title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open AI governance for research organizations AI governance people actually use. GovWren is an open system of record for AI governance: one front door for every AI request, review in proportion to the risk, a connected inventory of what your organization actually runs, and evidence behind every decision. It is built first for organizations where many labs and units adopt AI faster than any committee can track. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub A front door, not a gate A catalog answers "may I use this?" in seconds, and registering an everyday use takes a minute. The easy path is the governed one. In proportion A tier that explains itself decides who reviews, who decides, and how ofte

title: Overview
heading: "May I use this?" answered in seconds
text: Every tool and model your organization has evaluated is in one searchable catalog, with its standing, the data it may be used with, and its terms of use. Using an approved tool for everyday work is registered in a minute and approved on the spot. Reading the catalog → Requests

title: Overview
heading: A form that asks only what it needs
text: Anything new starts with a short form. Questions appear only when earlier answers call for them, and the likely risk tier is shown beside the form as it changes, with the reason for every part of it. Making a request → Review

title: Overview
heading: One packet, one decision
text: Rules route each request to the reviewers it needs, who work in parallel. Whoever decides sees one packet: the request, why it has its tier, every finding, and the discussion. Nobody reviews or decides their own request. The review queue → Decisions

title: Overview
heading: Every decision, with its reasons
text: A decision carries its rationale, the conditions it was made on, and who owns each one. Conditions that must be met before use hold the approval until they are, and evidence can be attached to show they were. Reading a decision → The inventory

title: Overview
heading: Models you run yourselves, on the record
text: Open weights on a lab workstation and models fine-tuned in-house are governed like anything else: where the weights came from, their checksum and license, where they run, and a model card. A model is never less sensitive than the data it was trained on. Models and datasets → Connections

title: Overview
heading: See what depends on what
text: Use cases, systems, models, datasets, and vendors are linked. When a supplier withdraws a model, one tab shows every system built on it and every use case that relies on those systems. The dependency graph → Your program

title: Overview
heading: Change the rules without a developer
text: The form, the tiers, the routing rules, and the vocabularies are edited in the app. Before publishing a change you see what it would have done to the requests already decided, and nothing that was decided is ever rewritten. Changing the program → Oversight

title: Overview
heading: Where the program stands, today
text: The dashboard counts approved uses by tier, unit, and area, open reviews by age, what is overdue, and how complete the records are. Every total and bar opens the records it counts. Reading the dashboard → Keeping watch

title: Overview
heading: An inventory that stays true
text: Sixty days before an approval ends, its owner is asked to confirm the answers given last time. If nothing that matters has changed, it is approved again on the spot. An approval nobody renews is marked lapsed, in the open, with the reason. Periodic reviews → Attestation

title: Overview
heading: Owners confirm in a few clicks
text: A campaign asks every owner whether each record is still true, and every steward whether their unit's list is complete. Coverage is counted by unit, with who has yet to answer. A record reported as changed goes straight into a change declaration. Attestation campaigns → Incidents

title: Overview
heading: When something goes wrong, everything that depends on it knows
text: Anyone can report an incident or a near miss. Governance triages it, may suspend an approval or open a review, and sets actions with owners and dates. An incident on a model shows on every system built on it and every use of those systems. Incidents and actions → The committee

title: Overview
heading: Meetings with an agenda, decisions, and minutes
text: Reviews that a committee decides are gathered into a session. Each decision is recorded as made there, and a closed session cannot be changed. Where the rules require it, a named person accepts the risk before anything is approved. Committee sessions → Assurance

title: Overview
heading: Risks written down, scored, and owned
text: Draw a risk from a library written for research and health settings, score it before and after treatment, and name who owns it. A grid shows where open risks stand, and a high risk shows on everything that relies on its record. The risk register → Controls

title: Overview
heading: Safeguards defined once, shown with their evidence
text: Thirty controls say what a governance program has to do. Each applies to the program or to every record its rule picks out, and has a standing, an owner, evidence, and a date it is next checked. Evidence that runs out becomes someone's action. The control library → Frameworks, if you need one

title: Overview
heading: Readiness that is worked out, not typed in
text: Load a framework as a data file and see each requirement as covered, partly covered, a gap, or not mapped, from how your controls stand. Nothing needs a framework, and no single percentage hides the gaps. Frameworks and readiness → An unbroken record

title: Overview
heading: History that cannot be quietly changed
text: Every change to every record is written to an append-only history, with who, when, and each value before and after. Entries are chained by hash, and one command proves that nothing was altered or removed. Trusting the history → Your sign-in Single sign-on with Microsoft Entra ID or any OpenID Connect provider, with roles from its groups. Single sign-on → Your server SQLite on a laptop or PostgreSQL in production, one process, and a data home you can back up as a whole. Configuration → Your brand Your name, logo, and accent color, three palettes, light and dark, with contrast checked as you choose. Make it yours → Checked Every screen audited for accessibility in every palette, by day and aft

title: Overview
heading: Try it in a minute
text: GovWren needs uv , which provides Python 3.12 or newer. The demo builds an invented medical research institute with thirty months of history: 66 units, about 260 people, 60 models, 70 datasets, and 300 use cases with their reviews, decisions, and evidence. git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/govwren.git cd govwren uv sync uv run govwren demo uv run govwren --config demo/govwren.toml serve Then open http://127.0.0.1:8010 and choose who to sign in as. To set GovWren up for your own organization, start with Getting started .

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from nothing to a running GovWren that your organization can sign in to. It is for whoever installs it and sets it up. Allow about fifteen minutes. If you only want to look around first, skip to Explore the demo organization .

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: uv , which provides the right Python (3.12 or later). A copy of this repository. Every command in these guides is run through uv run govwren … from the repository directory. The full list is in the command reference .

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: uv sync

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the installation
text: uv run govwren init init does five things: Writes govwren.toml , the deployment settings, in the current directory. Creates the data home, ./var , which holds everything that is not in the database. Creates the database. With no other setting, this is a SQLite file inside the data home. Loads the default program: the request form, the scoring model, the routing rules, and the standard conditions. Asks for your email address, your name, and a password, and creates the first administrator. The password needs at least 12 characters. Length matters more than symbols: a few unrelated words make a good one. It may not contain the name part of your email address. init is safe to run again. It leave

title: Getting started
heading: Check it
text: uv run govwren doctor doctor checks the configuration, the data home and its free space, that the database answers, that its schema is the one this version expects, that the database still refuses changes to the history, and that the history verifies. It exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Getting started
heading: Run it
text: uv run govwren serve The server prints its address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Use --port to pick another port. serve refuses to start in three cases, and says what to do in each: It says Do this The database schema is behind uv run govwren db upgrade There is no administrator yet uv run govwren users add you@example.org --name "Your Name" --role admin The port is already in use Stop what is using it, or pass --port As installed, GovWren listens only on the machine it runs on. To put it in front of other people, read Configuration first.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in for the first time
text: Open the address in a browser and sign in with the email address and password you gave init . Out of the box, people sign in with local accounts: an email address and a password held by GovWren. To let them use the account your organization already gives them, see Single sign-on . To send notices by email, see Email . Five failed attempts within fifteen minutes lock sign-in for that account for a few minutes. A sign-in ends after 12 hours without activity, and after 7 days in any case. Both are settings . To change your password, open the account menu at the top right and choose Your account . Changing it signs out your other sessions. If you cannot sign in at all, reset the password from th

heading: Find your way around

Section Pages Who sees them (top) Home, Catalog Everyone Inventory Use cases, AI systems, Vendors Everyone Governance Dashboard, Reviews Dashboard: governance, auditors, administrators. Reviews: those and reviewers Admin People, Units, Appearance Administrators The top bar has Go to… , New request , the bell for your notices, Appearance , and your account menu. Go to… opens the command palette. Press ⌘K on a Mac or Ctrl K elsewhere, or / when you are not typing in a field. Type to filter, use the arrow keys to move, and press Enter. Appearance sets light, dark, or system mode and one of three palettes (Wren, Slate, Garnet) for you alone. Th

title: Getting started
heading: Finish the setup checklist
text: Until the installation is set up, an administrator's Home shows a card, Set up your installation , with three steps. Each has a button that opens the right page.

title: Getting started
heading: 1. Describe your organization
text: Open Units . Every record in GovWren belongs to a unit, so this comes first. Choose Add your organization . This is the top unit. There is only one. Use Add within on any unit to add the divisions, departments, and labs beneath it. Units can nest to any depth. Give each unit a short, permanent Code , such as HALE . Imports match units by code. If you already have the structure in a spreadsheet, choose Import instead. See Import units and people from CSV . Admin → Units

title: Getting started
heading: 2. Add the people who will run the program
text: Open People and choose Add a person . Enter a name and an email address. Then either: set a password, and tell them what it is, so they can sign in at once; or leave the password empty. The person is added as invited . They can be named on records straight away, and can sign in once you set a password for them. Open a person to set the units they work in and their roles. Role What it is for Admin Accounts, units, appearance, and the installation itself Governance Running the program: triage, decisions, the catalog, any record Reviewer Review tasks for the review functions they are given Auditor Reading everything, changing nothing Steward Looking after the records of one unit and the units w

title: Getting started
heading: 3. Make it yours
text: Open Appearance to set the product name, your organization's name, a default palette, an accent color, and your logos. A preview shows your choices before you save. See Set the appearance . The checklist marks a step done when there is at least one unit, when there is more than one account, and when an organization name, logo, or accent color has been set. Admin → Appearance

title: Getting started
heading: What to do next
text: Add the AI tools your organization has already evaluated to the catalog, so people get an answer the first time they look. See Running the program . Read the default risk tiers and routing rules, and decide whether they suit you. See Running the program . Point people at Requesting , and reviewers at Reviewing .

title: Getting started
heading: Explore the demo organization
text: The demo is a complete, fictional organization: the Alderpoint Institute for Medical Research. It has thirty months of history, with 66 units four levels deep, about 260 people, 40 vendors, 90 AI systems, and 300 use cases at every stage, tier, and standing. uv run govwren demo uv run govwren --config demo/govwren.toml serve The first command builds the demo in ./demo , with its own configuration, data home, and database. It does not touch your own installation. The second starts it on port 8010. The sign-in page of a demo lists nine sample people. Choose one to sign in as them; no password is asked for. Between them they cover every role: an administrator, two people in governance, a privac

title: Getting started
heading: SQLite or PostgreSQL
text: GovWren runs on either, with the same features and the same data model. SQLite PostgreSQL Set up Nothing to do. It is the default Needs a server, a database, and one setting Where the data is One file, var/govwren.db The database server Good for Trying it out, a pilot, a small team Many people at once, more than one server process Back up The data home, as a whole The database, and the data home Start with SQLite unless you already know you need PostgreSQL. Configuration shows how to set PostgreSQL up.

title: Getting started
heading: Keep it healthy
text: To Run Check the installation uv run govwren doctor Check that the history has not been altered uv run govwren verify See which schema the database is at uv run govwren db current Apply schema changes after updating GovWren uv run govwren db upgrade List accounts, or get back in when nobody can sign in uv run govwren users list , uv run govwren users reset-password EMAIL Back up before db upgrade . An upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring.

title: Requesting
heading: Requesting
text: Requesting This guide is for researchers and staff who want to use an AI tool. It covers looking a tool up, registering an everyday use, making a request, and what happens afterwards. The short version: Look the tool up in the catalog. If it is approved and your use is an everyday one, register it. That takes about a minute and is approved at once. If not, make a request. A short form works out a risk tier, and the tier decides how much review the request gets.

title: Requesting
heading: Ask "May I use this AI tool?"
text: Home has a card with that question. Type the name of a tool and choose Look it up . You land in the catalog, filtered to what you typed. Home also lists what is Waiting on you : requests you have not finished, questions from reviewers, and conditions you own, with anything overdue first. The bell in the top bar holds your notices. Home, for a researcher

title: Requesting
heading: Read the catalog
text: The Catalog lists the AI tools your organization has evaluated. Search it by tool or vendor name. Each entry shows: On the entry What it means Standing Approved , Approved with restrictions , Under evaluation , or Not approved Data The most sensitive class of data the tool may be used with, such as "Up to Internal" Not for Kinds of data it must never be used with Training Whether the supplier trains on what you enter, where that is known Terms of use The conditions that apply to everyone who uses it A standing applies to one edition of a product. A free edition and an enterprise edition of the same tool are separate entries and can have different standings, so check the edition under the nam

title: Requesting
heading: Register a use of an approved tool
text: On an approved tool, choose Register my use . The form asks: Field What to enter What will you use it for? A short name, such as "Drafting grant summaries" Which unit is this for? Your lab, department, or office The most sensitive data involved One data class. The form reminds you what the tool is approved for Does it involve any of these? Tick any kinds of data that apply How will it be used? Tick the box if it only produces drafts, summaries, or answers that a person checks Choose Register . One of two things happens. It is registered and approved at once when all of these are true: the data class is no more sensitive than the tool is approved for; none of the kinds of data you ticked is e

title: Requesting
heading: Make a request
text: Choose New request in the top bar. The default form is called "Request to use AI" and takes about five minutes. Your organization may have changed its questions.

title: Requesting
heading: Fill in the form
text: The form is in sections, listed on the left. The first three are always there: Section Asks about The basics What you will use AI for, which unit, a description, the tool, how far along it is People and decisions Who is affected, how serious a mistake could be, how the output is used, whether it acts by itself, who checks it Data The most sensitive class of data, kinds of data, where the data goes, how widely it will be used More sections appear only when your answers call for them: Section Appears when Data about people You tick personal, health, human-subjects, genetic, or student data The supplier The data goes to an outside supplier Actions it can take The tool can take actions by itself

title: Requesting
heading: Watch the likely tier
text: Beside the form, Likely tier shows the risk tier your answers point to, once you have answered a few questions. It lists each of the six factors with its level and the answer that set it, and updates as you change answers. Below it, What happens next says what will follow if you submit now: approval on the spot, or which reviews are needed, who decides, and the usual number of working days. The tier is confirmed when you submit. The preview and the recorded tier use the same rules. The request form, with the likely tier beside it

title: Requesting
heading: Save a draft and come back
text: There is no save button. Once you have said what the request is for and which unit it belongs to, your answers are saved as you go, and the form shows Saved as with the request's reference, such as UC-0142 . To pick a draft up later, on any device, open Finish your request under Waiting on you on Home, or find it under Use cases with the Mine filter and choose Continue the request . A draft is seen only by you and by the people who may read every record.

title: Requesting
heading: Submit
text: Submit request is on the last section. If required questions are unanswered, the form takes you to the first one. When you submit, GovWren records your answers, works out the tier, and applies the routing rules. The answers are now part of the record. You can read them on the use case under the Answers tab, along with the version of the form you answered.

title: Requesting
heading: What the tier means
text: Each of six factors scores from 0 to 3: impact on people, decision role, autonomy, data sensitivity, data exposure, and reach. The total gives the tier. With the default program: Tier What it is What happens Minimal Everyday use with little that can go wrong Approved on submission, by rule, with standard conditions, unless an answer calls for a review Moderate Some sensitivity Governance decides, usually within 5 working days High Real potential for harm Privacy and security review; the governance committee decides, usually within 15 working days Critical Serious potential for harm Privacy, security, and legal review; the committee decides and an executive accepts the risk, usually within 30

title: Requesting
heading: Follow your request
text: Open the use case from Use cases or from a notice. Its standing is shown under the name: Standing Meaning Draft Not submitted yet In review Submitted; with governance or reviewers With requester Waiting on you Approved Approved, with no conditions Approved with conditions Approved, with conditions to keep to Declined Not approved; the reason is on the record Withdrawn You took it back The Review card says who it is waiting on, the target date, and which reviews are waiting or done. You see where each review stands. You do not see reviewers' findings or the notes they write among themselves.

title: Requesting
heading: Answer a reviewer's question
text: When reviewers need something from you, the request moves to With requester , you get a notice, and Home shows Answer a question . The review clock is stopped while it waits on you. On the use case, under Discussion , you can do either of these: Write a reply and choose Send reply . The request goes back to the reviewers. Choose Update your answers to reopen the form, change what needs changing, and submit again. The tier is worked out again from the new answers. You can also write in the discussion at any time while the review is open. Everything you write there is seen by the reviewers.

title: Requesting
heading: Read the decision
text: When the request is decided you get a notice, and the card on the use case becomes Decision . It shows the outcome, the reason, who decided and when. A decision is never edited afterwards. An approval that was made by rule says so. An approval runs until the Approved until date shown on the use case. With the default program that is 36 months for Minimal, 24 for Moderate, 12 for High, and 6 for Critical. If a request is declined, the reason says why. You can make a new request, for example with an approved tool. A decided request: the decision, its conditions, and the tier's reasons

title: Requesting
heading: Keep to the conditions
text: Approvals usually carry conditions. Each has an owner, by default the accountable owner of the use case, and one of three kinds: Kind Meaning Before use Must be met before you start. Until then the approval is Not in effect yet By a date Must be met by the date shown Ongoing Something to keep to for as long as you use the tool To mark a condition as met, open the use case, find it under Conditions , and choose Met . Say how it was met; the note is kept on the record. Owners of the use case, stewards of its unit, and governance can do this. Only governance can waive a condition. To show how a condition was met, choose Attach beside it before you mark it as met, and add a file, an address, or

title: Requesting
heading: After the approval
text: An approval has an end date, and it covers the use as you described it. Before the end date you are asked to confirm your answers. See Confirm your answers . If what you do changes, say so. See Declare a change . If the use ends, retire it. See Retire a record . If something goes wrong, or nearly does, report it. See Report an incident .

title: Requesting
heading: Withdraw a request
text: You can take a request back while its review is open. Open the use case and choose Withdraw this request at the foot of its Review card. The review is closed and the use case is marked Withdrawn. You can make a new request later.

title: Requesting
heading: Who can see your request
text: A draft is seen only by you and by the people who may read every record: governance, auditors, and administrators. A request in review is also seen by its owners, the stewards and members of its unit, and the reviewers whose review it needs. Once approved, how much the rest of the organization sees is a setting. By default, everyone sees a summary and your own unit sees it in full.

title: Reviewing
heading: Reviewing
text: Reviewing This guide is for the people on the reviewing side of a request: governance, who triage and decide; reviewers, who record findings for their function; and auditors, who read. For how a request is made, see Requesting . For how tiers and routing rules are set, see Running the program .

title: Reviewing
heading: How a review moves
text: When a request is submitted, GovWren works out its tier and applies the routing rules. If no rule requires a review and one approves it, the request is approved on the spot and never reaches the queue. Otherwise a review is opened, with a reference such as RV-0087 , and moves through these states: State Waiting on What happens Waiting for triage Governance Governance confirms or adjusts the reviews the rules require With reviewers Reviewers Each required review function records a finding. They work in parallel With the requester The requester Someone asked a question, or the request was returned Ready for a decision Governance Every review is finished Decided Nobody Approved, declined, or wi

title: Reviewing
heading: Work the review queue
text: Open Reviews . The list on the left holds the reviews you have a part in, soonest due first. The one you select opens on the right. Each item in the list shows the request's name, its tier, the state of the review, its reference and unit, how many reviews are finished, and when it is due. A dot marks the ones waiting on you, and Yours: names the review tasks that are yours to do. The page opens on the first one that needs you. Press J or the down arrow for the next review, and K or the up arrow for the previous one. The keys do nothing while you are typing in a field or have a dialog open. Open shows reviews still in progress. All adds the ones already decided. The address changes as you mov

title: Reviewing
heading: Read the packet
text: Everything about a request is on one screen: Part What it holds Header The request's name, tier, state, target date, and who opened it and when The request Its description, unit, owners, data class and kinds of data, the AI systems it uses with their catalog standing, and the oversight described. See every answer opens the full form Why this tier Each factor's level and the answer that set it, the points, any floor that raised the tier, and any stop Reviews One task for each required review function: who has it, and what they found Discussion Notes among reviewers, and messages to and from the requester A reviewer sees the whole request, whatever unit it belongs to. A line at the foot shows

title: Reviewing
heading: Triage a request
text: Triage is for governance. A request waiting for triage shows a Triage card. Read the request and why it has its tier. Under Required by the rules , each review is ticked and names the rule that required it. Untick one that is not needed here. Open Require another review to add a function the rules did not ask for. If you changed anything, write a Reason for the change . It is kept on the record. Choose Confirm and start . The reviewers for each function are notified, and the review moves to With reviewers. If no review is required, it goes straight to Ready for a decision. A review is triaged once. A review that was removed at triage is shown as Not required , with your reason.

title: Reviewing
heading: Do a review task
text: Under Reviews , find the task for your function. Choose Take it to put your name on the task, so others know it is in hand. This is optional; recording a finding also puts your name on it. Choose Record finding and pick one: Finding Meaning What you must add No concerns Nothing in your area stands in the way Nothing Acceptable with conditions Acceptable if the conditions you name are attached The conditions, and notes explaining them Objection It should not go ahead as proposed Notes explaining why For conditions, tick any under More standard conditions , or choose Write another condition and say what is required and when. Write your Notes , then choose Record finding . Your notes and findin

title: Reviewing
heading: Attach what you relied on
text: Choose Attach on your task to add a file, an address, or a note to your review: a supplier's report you read, a test you ran. It is kept with the task and shown to the people who can read reviewers' notes, never to the requester.

title: Reviewing
heading: Use the discussion
text: The Discussion has two audiences. Choose one before you write: Choice Who sees it Reviewers only Governance, the reviewers on this review, auditors, and administrators. Never the requester To the requester Everyone on the review, including the requester, who gets a notice Reviewers only is selected to begin with. Messages for reviewers only are marked as such in the thread.

title: Reviewing
heading: Ask a question that stops the clock
text: To ask the requester for something, choose To the requester , tick Ask the requester, and pause the clock until they reply , write the question, and choose Add . The review moves to With the requester, and the requester is notified. The time it spends there is counted separately. It is left out of the figure for time with reviewers and out of the dashboard's median time to a decision. The target date itself does not move. The review returns to where it was when the requester replies, or updates their answers and submits again. If they update their answers, the tier is worked out again and a note in the discussion gives the new tier. Reviewers can still record findings while a request is with

title: Reviewing
heading: Change a tier
text: The tier is worked out from the answers, but the answers do not always tell the whole story. A reviewer or governance can change it. Open the use case, for example from the request's name at the top of the packet. On the Why this tier card, choose Change . Pick the tier and write a Reason : why the worked-out tier is wrong for this request. Choose Change tier . The reason is required and is shown beside the tier from then on, with your name. The tier that was worked out is kept, so the record shows both. A tier can be raised or lowered. Changing a tier does not re-route a review that is already open. The reviews it needs are the ones set by the rules when it was submitted, as adjusted at tri

title: Reviewing
heading: Decide
text: Deciding is for governance. Once a request has been triaged, a bar above the packet shows who decides and what the review is waiting on, with three buttons. Button When you can use it Result Approve… Only when the review is Ready for a decision Approved, or Approved with conditions Return… Any time, unless it is already with the requester Goes back to the requester with your question. The review stays open Decline… Any time Declined. The review is closed Every decision needs a reason. It is shown to the requester and kept on the record. A decision is never edited afterwards. The bar says on whose authority the decision is made: governance, the governance committee, or the committee with an e

title: Reviewing
heading: Approve
text: Choose Approve… and write the Reason for the decision . Under Conditions , the ones the rules attach and the ones reviewers recommended are already ticked, each marked with where it came from. Untick any that should not apply. Open More standard conditions to add others, or choose Write another condition . Choose Approve . If a reviewer objected, the form warns you. You can still approve, but say in your reason how the objection is answered. The record will show the decision was Made over an objection . The approval runs for the number of months the rules give the tier, shown as Approved until . A prohibited use cannot be approved.

title: Reviewing
heading: Return
text: Choose Return… and say what you need from the requester. Your words are sent to them as a question, and the clock stops until they reply. Use this when the request cannot be decided as written, but could be with changes.

title: Reviewing
heading: Decline
text: Choose Decline… and give the reason. Be specific: the requester reads it, and it is the record of why.

title: Reviewing
heading: Set conditions
text: A condition is something the requester must do or keep to. Each has an owner and one of three kinds. Kind Use it for Effect Before use Something that must be true before the tool is used at all The approval is held: the use case shows Not in effect yet until every before-use condition is met or waived By a date A task with a deadline Shown as overdue once the date passes. A date is required Ongoing A rule to keep to for as long as the use continues Stays open as a standing obligation The owner is the accountable owner of the use case unless you say otherwise. Before-use and by-date conditions appear on their owner's Home until closed. Conditions are closed on the use case page, under Conditi

title: Reviewing
heading: Reviews that come later
text: Not every review is of a new request. The eyebrow of the packet says which kind it is. Kind Why it opened What is different Periodic review The approval is about to end It starts with the owner, who confirms the answers. See Periodic reviews Change review The owner declared a material change The packet shows each answer before and after. title: Reviewing
heading: The two rules that always hold
text: Nobody triages, reviews, or decides their own request. If you made a request, or are one of its owners, you cannot triage it, take or complete a review task on it, change its tier, or decide it. Your role makes no difference: this holds for governance too. Someone else with the role must act. The same check stops a review task being assigned to one of the request's owners. What reviewers say among themselves is never shown to the requester. Findings, reviewers' notes, recommended conditions, and messages marked Reviewers only are left out of everything the requester sees: the use case page, the review, and the history. This also holds whatever the requester's role. A governance lead who make

title: Reviewing
heading: What auditors can and cannot do
text: The auditor role is for reading. An auditor can: open every use case, AI system, and vendor in full, including drafts and restricted records; open Reviews and read every review, including findings, reviewers' notes, and the whole discussion; read the History tab of any record; open the Dashboard and follow its totals and bars to their records; see every account, with its roles and units. An auditor cannot: triage, take a task, record a finding, or decide; write in a discussion; change a tier, or close or waive a condition; edit any record, unless they are also one of its owners. title: Running the program
heading: Running the program
text: Running the program This guide is for governance leads and administrators. It covers who can do what, how to describe your organization, how to build the catalog, how tiers and routing work, how to change them, and how to read the dashboard and the history. Two roles share this work. Administrators manage people, units, and appearance. Governance runs the program: the catalog, triage, and decisions. One person can hold both.

Read and edit every record, including catalog standing Governance Whole organization Triage, decide, waive conditions, change tiers, edit any record, set catalog standing, see the dashboard Reviewer One or more review functions, or every function Take review tasks for those functions, record findings, write in discussions, change tiers Auditor Whole organization Read every record, review, and history, and the dashboard. Change nothing Steward A unit and every unit beneath it See and edit that unit's rec

title: Running the program
heading: Manage people
text: Under Admin → People , open a person to change their name, title, units, and roles, to Reset password , or to Disable them. A disabled person is signed out and cannot sign in. Their records and everything they did stay in the history. The same can be done from the command line, which is how you get back in when nobody can sign in: uv run govwren users add wei.chen@alderpoint.example --name "Wei Chen" --role reviewer=function:privacy uv run govwren users roles priya.nair@alderpoint.example --set steward=unit:HALE uv run govwren users list See the command reference for every option.

title: Running the program
heading: Units
text: Every use case belongs to a unit, and stewards look after a unit and everything beneath it. Units are managed under Admin → Units . There is one top unit, the organization itself. Every other unit sits within another. A unit has a name, a kind (such as division, department, or lab), and an optional code. A unit can be renamed or moved. It cannot be moved beneath itself. A unit is never deleted. Set its status to Closed : it keeps its records and history and can no longer be chosen.

title: Running the program
heading: Import units and people from CSV
text: Both Units and People have an Import button. Save your spreadsheet as CSV in UTF-8, with a header row. Choose the file, then Check the file . Nothing is changed. Read the report: how many rows would be added, changed, or left as they are, and every problem with its row number. Fix the file until there are no problems, then choose Import . Nothing is imported unless every row is good. A file can hold up to 20,000 rows and 5 MB. Units. Matched by code, so importing again updates them. title: Running the program

Under How it handles data , record whether the supplier trains on what is entered, how long inputs are kept, and where data is processed.

Choose how many steps to follow. The same records are listed under the picture, each with how it is connected and how many steps away it is, so nothing is shown only as a drawing. Use it when something changes. When a supplier withdraws a model, open the model's Connections tab to see every AI system built on it and every use case that uses those systems. title: Running the program
heading: A model is as sensitive as its training data
text: A model can reproduce what it was trained on. When you link a model to a dataset with Trained on , the model's sensitivity is raised to the dataset's data class if it was lower. The same follows through Derived from : a model fine-tuned from another is at least as sensitive as everything in its line. The model's page says which datasets set the level, and nobody can set it lower.

title: Running the program
heading: Describe an agent
text: An AI system whose kind is Agent has a card, What it can do by itself : how much it does without a person, what it can change and where, the tools it is connected to, the account it acts as, whether its actions can be undone, how a person stops it, what it remembers, and its limits. An agent with none of this recorded shows a warning. An agent's profile

title: Running the program
heading: Keep vendor agreements
text: A vendor's page lists its Agreements : the kind, a title, your reference, the dates it runs between, the notice it needs, whether it renews by itself, and who looks after it. Each shows where it stands today: Shown as Means Current In force, with time to spare Ends soon Ends within 90 days In its notice period The last day to give notice has passed or is today Ended Past its end date and does not renew by itself A vendor and its agreements

text: Evidence is whatever shows that a thing is so: an approval letter, a signed agreement, a supplier's assurance report, a test result. Every record has an Evidence card, and so does every condition and every review task. Choose Attach and give: Field Meaning What is it? title: Running the program
heading: Point to other systems
text: Every record has an In other systems card for the protocol, grant, agreement, purchase, ticket, or repository it belongs to: a kind, the number or name used there, and optionally a label and an address. GovWren stores the pointer and nothing else.

title: Running the program
heading: Find things and keep the inventory tidy

title: Running the program
heading: Search everything
text: Press <kbd>⌘K</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl K</kbd>, or choose the search box at the top, and type. Records of every kind that match are listed as you type, with pages and actions beneath them: use cases, AI systems, models, datasets, vendors, and evidence. Type a whole reference, such as MDL-0048 , and that record comes first. You are shown only what you may see.

title: Running the program
heading: Save a view
text: Every list keeps its filters and sort in its address, so a filtered list can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague. To keep one for yourself, set the filters you want and choose Save view . Your views are in the Saved views menu on that list. Choose one to apply it; when the list matches a view, Remove view appears. Views are your own: nobody else sees them.

title: Running the program
heading: See what a record is missing
text: Every record's page has a Completeness card: a percentage, and a plain list of what is still to record. What is expected depends on the record. A model you run yourselves is expected to say where its weights came from and what their checksum is; an agent is expected to say how a person stops it; a vendor you are a customer of is expected to have an agreement on file. The dashboard shows the average for each kind of record. It leaves out drafts and retired records.

title: Running the program
heading: Merge duplicates
text: Duplicates , under Governance, lists records that look like the same thing entered twice, by how alike their names are. Two editions of one product are different systems, and two versions of one model are different models; neither is listed. To merge a pair, choose Keep this one on the record that should stay. Everything that pointed to the other record now points to the one you kept: links, evidence, references, and the people named as technical owners or contacts. For a vendor, its AI systems, models, and agreements move too. The other record is kept, marked as retired, with a notice that leads to the one that took its place, so its reference still works wherever it was written down. A mer

heading: Bring existing records in, and take lists out

title: Running the program
heading: Import from a spreadsheet
text: If you already keep a list of AI tools, vendors, models, or datasets, import it. On the list for that kind of record, choose Import (governance only). Save the spreadsheet as CSV, with a header row. Choose the file. GovWren reads the header and guesses which column is which field. Correct the guesses under Which column is which? Set a column to Leave out to ignore it. One column must be the Name. Choose Check the file . Every row is tried and nothing is kept. The report says how many records would be added and changed, and lists every problem with its row. Fix the file and check again until there are no problems, then choose Import . How cells are read: Field What to write A choice, such as

title: Running the program
heading: Export a list
text: Every list has an Export… menu. It downloads the list as it is filtered now, every page of it, as CSV for a spreadsheet or as JSON. The file holds only what you may see. The first line of a CSV export begins with # and says what the file is, when it was made, and the filters that produced it. GovWren's own import skips that line; delete it if another program objects. JSON exports carry the same in their export and filters fields. Cells that a spreadsheet would run as a formula are written as plain text.

title: Running the program
heading: The data classes
text: GovWren ships with four data classes, ordered from least to most sensitive. The order matters: catalog permissions compare against it. Class Definition Public Poses little or no risk if disclosed, and may be shared with anyone Internal Meant for use inside the organization, by its own people, for its own work. Not to be shared outside without oversight Protected Could harm people or the organization if seen by the wrong person, inside or out. Access is limited to those who need it for their work Restricted Governed by specific legal, regulatory, or contractual obligations. Loss or disclosure may require notifying people, partners, or authorities Each class carries examples, grouped as Person

text: The default scoring model has six factors. Each scores 0 to 3, and takes the highest level any answer gives it. heading: Routing rules
text: Routing rules turn a tiered request into a review. Each rule has a condition, on the tier or on answers, and effects. Rules are read in order and their effects add up. Besides the four tier rules above, the default rules add reviews for particular answers. Two of them concern models people run or train themselves: any such model needs an information security review and must be recorded in the inventory before use, and a model trained on Protected or Restricted data also needs a data stewardship review. You work on a copy. Nothing you change is in force until you publish it, and the bar at the top of the page says what you have changed. Discard changes throws the copy away.

title: Running the program
heading: The tiers
text: Each factor scores from 0 to 3, the points are added up, and the total decides the tier. On the Tiers tab you set: what each tier is called and the total it begins at; for each factor, the rules that raise it: a score, when it applies, and the reason shown beside the factor; floors , which set the least a tier can be whatever the points come to; prohibited uses , which cannot be approved at all. Editing the tiers

title: Running the program
heading: The routing rules
text: Every rule that applies to a request adds to what happens to it. On the Routing rules tab, each rule has a name, when it applies, the reviews it requires, who decides, the target in working days, how often an approval is looked at again, the standard conditions it attaches, and whether it approves at once when nothing else requires a review. The standard conditions are below the rules: the wording, and whether each is before use, by a date, or ongoing. Editing the routing rules

title: Running the program
heading: Conditions, in words
text: Wherever the program asks "when?", you build the answer as a sentence: choose what it is about (a question in the form, or the tier), how it compares, and the value. Add tests and say whether all of them or any of them must hold.

title: Running the program
heading: The vocabularies
text: The lists that records and forms choose from. Rename a value freely: records hold its permanent key, so nothing is rewritten. Add values, and put them in order. A value that records may already hold cannot be removed; tick Retired and it stays on the records that have it and is no longer offered. Editing a vocabulary

title: Running the program
heading: Check, then publish
text: Check does two things and changes nothing. It checks the whole program for mistakes: a rule about a question that no longer exists, a choice with no label, two questions stored under one name. Every problem is listed. It runs the requests already submitted through your working copy and says what would have come out differently: how many would have had a higher or lower tier, needed different reviews, or moved between approval by rule and review by people, with examples you can open. Publish is offered once a check has passed. Each part you changed becomes a new version. Earlier versions are kept, and the Versions tab lists them with who published each and when. Publishing never changes what

title: Running the program
heading: People asking for tools
text: When someone cannot find a tool in the catalog, they can Ask for a tool to be evaluated : its name, what they want it for, and its website. The tool is added to AI systems, outside the catalog, and governance is told. If several people ask about the same tool, their requests are gathered under it. Those who keep the catalog see Tools people have asked about at the top of the catalog, most asked-for first. When you set the tool's catalog standing to approved, approved with restrictions, or not approved, everyone who asked is told. Tools people have asked about

Each record's History tab shows it in plain words. Changes made at the command line are recorded as such. To check the chain: uv run govwren verify It reports how many events hold, or the first event that has been altered, removed, or cut from the end, and exits with 1 if the history is broken. uv run govwren doctor runs the same check along with the rest.
